title: Walk Along Every Road Exactly Once

concept.title: Euler: a closed walk that uses every edge once exists when all degrees are even and the edges are connected
body: The seven bridges of Königsberg started graph theory. Is there a walk that uses **every edge exactly once** and ends where it began (an *Euler circuit*)? Euler found a simple rule. Every time the walk passes through a node, it enters by one edge and leaves by another, so it uses the edges of that node **in pairs**: the node must have an **even degree**. The start node is also left once and entered once at the end. So **all degrees must be even**.

That is also enough, with one more condition: all the edges must belong to **one connected piece**. (Isolated nodes without edges do not matter, because the walk has no business there.) Two separate triangles have all degrees even, but one walk cannot visit both.

body.code:
degree = [0] * (n + 1)
for u, v in edges:
    degree[u] += 1
    degree[v] += 1
all_even = all(d % 2 == 0 for d in degree)

# search from the end of any edge and count the nodes with edges that were reached
reached = ...   # nodes with degree > 0 reached from edges[0][0]
wanted = sum(1 for d in degree if d > 0)
answer = all_even and reached == wanted

body: The check costs O(n + m). Finding the circuit itself (Hierholzer's algorithm) is a harder task of this topic; here only its existence is asked, which shows how a global property can follow from a local one (the degrees).

statement: An undirected graph has `n` nodes and `m >= 1` edges. Is there a closed walk that uses every edge exactly once? (A node can be visited many times.) Print `yes` or `no`.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `m`: the number of nodes (numbered 1 to n) and the number of edges.
Each of the next `m` lines has two numbers `u` and `v`: an edge between the nodes `u` and `v`.
constraints: There are no self-loops and no repeated edges.

examples.note: Two separate triangles: every degree is even, but one walk cannot cover both: no.

hints: Compute the degrees: all of them must be even.
The edges must be connected: search from one end of the first edge and count the reached nodes that have edges.
Compare with the number of nodes that have at least one edge.

explanation: An Euler circuit exists exactly when every degree is even and all the nodes that have edges are connected: the degrees are checked, then a search from the end of the first edge must reach all nodes with degree above zero.
solution.complexity: Time O(n + m), space O(n + m).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, m = map(int, input().split())
edges = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(m)]

adj = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
for u, v in edges:
    adj[u].append(v)
    adj[v].append(u)
degree = [len(adj[v]) for v in range(n + 1)]
ok = all(d % 2 == 0 for d in degree)
if ok:
    seen = [False] * (n + 1)
    start = edges[0][0]
    seen[start] = True
    queue = [start]
    for v in queue:
        for w in adj[v]:
            if not seen[w]:
                seen[w] = True
                queue.append(w)
    ok = len(queue) == sum(1 for d in degree if d > 0)
print("yes" if ok else "no")
